topic.subject: Chemistry
topic.title: Organic Analysis: Tests, Mass Spectrometry and IR

cards.q: Describe the test for a C=C double bond and give the result.
cards.a: Shake with bromine water. An alkene turns it from orange to colourless.

answerFigure.alt: Ethene adds bromine across its double bond to form 1,2-dibromoethane.

cards.why: Bromine adds across the C=C (electrophilic addition), so the orange colour disappears. An alkane gives no change.

cards.q: True or false: a positive result with bromine water is that it "goes clear".
cards.a: False. It goes colourless.
cards.why: Bromine water is already clear (transparent) but orange. "Clear" is not accepted for "colourless".

cards.q: Describe Tollens' test for an aldehyde and give the results for an aldehyde and a ketone.
cards.a: Warm with Tollens' reagent (ammoniacal silver nitrate) in a water bath. An aldehyde gives a silver mirror; a ketone gives no change.

figure.alt: Ethanal is oxidised by Tollens’ reagent to ethanoic acid.

cards.why: The aldehyde is oxidised; \(\mathrm{Ag^{+}}\) is reduced to silver: \(\mathrm{Ag^{+} + e^{-} \rightarrow Ag}\).

cards.q: Describe the test for an aldehyde using Fehling's (or Benedict's) solution.
cards.a: Warm with the solution in a water bath. An aldehyde changes it from blue to a brick-red precipitate; a ketone gives no change.
cards.why: The aldehyde is oxidised; blue \(\mathrm{Cu^{2+}}\) is reduced to red copper(I) oxide, \(\mathrm{Cu_{2}O}\).

cards.q: What is seen when acidified potassium dichromate(VI) is warmed with a primary, a secondary and a tertiary alcohol?
cards.a: Primary and secondary: orange to green. Tertiary: stays orange.

figure.alt: Skeletal formulae of three isomers of C4H10O: butan-1-ol, a primary alcohol with OH on an end carbon; butan-2-ol, a secondary alcohol with OH on the second carbon; and 2-methylpropan-2-ol, a tertiary alcohol with OH on a carbon joined to three others.

cards.why: Orange \(\mathrm{Cr_{2}O_{7}^{2-}}\) is reduced to green \(\mathrm{Cr^{3+}}\). A tertiary alcohol has no H on the C–OH carbon, so it is not oxidised.

cards.q: Describe how to tell whether an unknown alcohol is primary, secondary or tertiary using chemical tests.
cards.a: Oxidise it, then test the product for an aldehyde.
marks: Warm the alcohol with acidified potassium dichromate(VI).
If it stays orange, the alcohol is tertiary.
If it turns green, distil off the product as it forms and test it with Tollens’ reagent (or Fehling’s solution).
A silver mirror (or red precipitate) shows an aldehyde, so the alcohol was primary.
No change shows a ketone, so the alcohol was secondary.

cards.q: Describe a test for a carboxylic acid and the result.
cards.a: Add sodium hydrogencarbonate (or sodium carbonate) solution. Effervescence: the gas, \(\mathrm{CO_{2}}\), turns limewater milky.

answerFigure.alt: Ethanoic acid reacts with sodium hydrogencarbonate to give sodium ethanoate, carbon dioxide and water.

cards.why: \(\mathrm{CH_{3}COOH + NaHCO_{3} \rightarrow CH_{3}COONa + CO_{2} + H_{2}O}\)

cards.q: Why does sodium hydrogencarbonate distinguish ethanoic acid from ethanol?
cards.a: Ethanoic acid is acidic enough to react with hydrogencarbonate and release CO<sub>2</sub>; ethanol is not, so it gives no fizzing.
cards.why: Alcohols are much weaker acids than water, so they do not react with carbonates.

cards.q: What is seen when phosphorus(V) chloride is added to a dry alcohol or carboxylic acid?
cards.a: Steamy (misty) fumes of hydrogen chloride, which turn damp blue litmus red.
cards.why: It shows an –OH group: \(\mathrm{CH_{3}CH_{2}OH + PCl_{5} \rightarrow CH_{3}CH_{2}Cl + POCl_{3} + HCl}\). The sample must be dry, because water also reacts.

cards.q: Why are organic test-tube reactions warmed in a water bath rather than over a Bunsen flame?
cards.a: Most organic compounds are flammable, so a naked flame must be avoided. A water bath also warms gently and evenly.
cards.why: Tollens’ reagent must also never be heated strongly or stored: make it fresh and dispose of it after use.

cards.q: Compound X, \(\mathrm{C_{3}H_{6}O}\), gives a silver mirror with Tollens' reagent. Name and draw X.
cards.a: Propanal

answerFigure.alt: Skeletal formula of propanal: a three-carbon chain ending in an aldehyde group.

cards.why: Its isomer propanone, \(\mathrm{CH_{3}COCH_{3}}\), is a ketone and gives no silver mirror.

cards.q: Compound Y, \(\mathrm{C_{3}H_{4}O_{2}}\), decolourises bromine water and fizzes with sodium hydrogencarbonate. Suggest its structure.
cards.a: Propenoic acid: it has a C=C and a COOH group.

answerFigure.alt: Skeletal formula of propenoic acid: a terminal C=C double bond joined to a carboxylic acid group.

cards.why: \(\mathrm{CH_{2}{=}CHCOOH}\). Each test identifies one functional group; together they fix the structure.

cards.q: Four unlabelled bottles contain ethanol, ethanal, ethanoic acid and cyclohexene. Plan a sequence of tests to identify each.
cards.a: One test per functional group, each giving a positive result with only one of the four.
marks: Add sodium hydrogencarbonate: fizzing (CO<sub>2</sub>, limewater milky) identifies ethanoic acid.
Add bromine water to the other three: orange to colourless identifies cyclohexene.
Warm the remaining two with Tollens’ reagent: a silver mirror identifies ethanal.
The last one is ethanol: confirm it turns acidified potassium dichromate(VI) from orange to green.

cards.q: What is the molecular ion peak in a mass spectrum, and what does it tell you?
cards.a: The peak made by the whole molecule having lost one electron, \(\mathrm{M^{+}}\). Its \(m/z\) value gives the relative molecular mass.
cards.why: It is the peak at the highest m/z, apart from a very small peak one unit higher caused by carbon-13.

cards.q: What is fragmentation, and why are only some fragments detected?
cards.a: The molecular ion breaks into a positive ion and a radical: \(\mathrm{M^{+} \rightarrow X^{+} + Y\bullet}\). Only the positive ion is detected.
cards.why: Radicals and neutral molecules are not charged, so they are not deflected or detected.

cards.q: Identify the fragment ions that could cause peaks at \(m/z\) 15, 29, 31, 43 and 45.
cards.why: Always include the positive charge when you identify a fragment.

cards.q: The mass spectrum of butane, \(\mathrm{C_{4}H_{10}}\), has a large peak at \(m/z = 43\). Write an equation for its formation.

figure.alt: Skeletal formula of butane, a straight four-carbon chain.

cards.a: \(\mathrm{C_{4}H_{10}^{+} \rightarrow C_{3}H_{7}^{+} + CH_{3}\bullet}\)
cards.why: \(M_{\text{r}} = 58\); losing a methyl radical (15) leaves the ion at 43.

cards.q: Propan-1-ol gives a peak at \(m/z = 31\). Write an equation for the fragmentation that forms it.

figure.alt: Skeletal formula of propan-1-ol: a three-carbon chain ending in OH.

cards.a: \(\mathrm{CH_{3}CH_{2}CH_{2}OH^{+} \rightarrow CH_{2}OH^{+} + CH_{3}CH_{2}\bullet}\)
cards.why: The C–C bond next to the OH breaks. Propan-2-ol cannot give \(\mathrm{CH_{2}OH^{+}}\) easily, so this peak helps tell the isomers apart.

cards.q: How could the mass spectra of propanal and propanone be used to tell them apart? Both have \(M_{\text{r}} = 58\).

figure.alt: Skeletal formula of propanone: a C=O group on the middle carbon of a three-carbon chain.

cards.a: Propanone gives a large peak at 43, \(\mathrm{CH_{3}CO^{+}}\), and at 15, \(\mathrm{CH_{3}^{+}}\). Propanal gives a large peak at 29, \(\mathrm{C_{2}H_{5}^{+}}\) or \(\mathrm{CHO^{+}}\).
cards.why: Isomers give the same molecular ion, so the fragmentation pattern must be used.

cards.q: Pentan-2-one and pentan-3-one both have \(M_{\text{r}} = 86\). Which peaks would show which isomer is present?

figure.alt: Skeletal formulae of pentan-2-one, with the C=O on the second carbon of a five-carbon chain, and pentan-3-one, with the C=O on the middle carbon.

cards.a: Pentan-3-one: 57, \(\mathrm{CH_{3}CH_{2}CO^{+}}\), and 29, \(\mathrm{C_{2}H_{5}^{+}}\). Pentan-2-one: 43, \(\mathrm{CH_{3}CO^{+}}\), and 71, \(\mathrm{CH_{3}CH_{2}CH_{2}CO^{+}}\).
cards.why: Ketones often break at a bond next to the C=O. Pentan-3-one is symmetrical, so both breaks give the same ions.

cards.q: A ketone has its molecular ion at \(m/z = 72\) and a large peak at 43. Identify the ketone.
cards.a: Butanone

answerFigure.alt: Skeletal formula of butanone: a four-carbon chain with C=O on the second carbon.

steps: The only ketone with this formula is butanone, \(\mathrm{CH_{3}COCH_{2}CH_{3}}\).
The peak at 43 is \(\mathrm{CH_{3}CO^{+}}\), consistent with this structure.
cards.why: Butanal is an isomer, but it is an aldehyde, not a ketone.

cards.q: Why can high-resolution mass spectrometry distinguish compounds with the same integer relative molecular mass?
cards.a: Precise atomic masses are not whole numbers (only carbon-12 is exactly 12), so compounds with different molecular formulae have slightly different precise masses.
cards.why: E.g. \(\mathrm{^{1}H}\) is 1.0078 and \(\mathrm{^{16}O}\) is 15.9949, so the differences show up in the third or fourth decimal place.

cards.q: A compound has a molecular ion peak at \(m/z = 44.0261\). Which formula fits: \(\mathrm{C_{3}H_{8}}\), \(\mathrm{CO_{2}}\) or \(\mathrm{C_{2}H_{4}O}\)? (\(\mathrm{^{1}H}\) 1.0078, \(\mathrm{^{12}C}\) 12.0000, \(\mathrm{^{16}O}\) 15.9949)
cards.a: \(\mathrm{C_{2}H_{4}O}\)
cards.why: All three have an integer Mr of 44; only the precise mass separates them.

cards.q: A ketone gives a molecular ion at \(m/z = 58.0417\). Show that its formula is \(\mathrm{C_{3}H_{6}O}\) and not \(\mathrm{C_{4}H_{10}}\) or \(\mathrm{C_{2}H_{2}O_{2}}\). (\(\mathrm{^{1}H}\) 1.0078, \(\mathrm{^{12}C}\) 12.0000, \(\mathrm{^{16}O}\) 15.9949)
cards.a: \(\mathrm{C_{3}H_{6}O}\) = 58.0417, matching the peak.
cards.why: The ketone is propanone, \(\mathrm{CH_{3}COCH_{3}}\).

cards.a: \(\mathrm{C_{2}H_{4}}\) (ethene)
cards.why: Hydrogen-rich formulae have precise masses slightly above the integer; oxygen-rich ones slightly below.

cards.q: A compound with molecular ion at \(m/z = 60.0210\) fizzes with sodium carbonate. Choose from \(\mathrm{C_{3}H_{8}O}\), \(\mathrm{C_{2}H_{4}O_{2}}\) and \(\mathrm{CH_{4}N_{2}O}\), and identify it. (\(\mathrm{^{1}H}\) 1.0078, \(\mathrm{^{12}C}\) 12.0000, \(\mathrm{^{14}N}\) 14.0031, \(\mathrm{^{16}O}\) 15.9949)
cards.a: \(\mathrm{C_{2}H_{4}O_{2}}\): ethanoic acid.

answerFigure.alt: Skeletal formula of ethanoic acid: a methyl group joined to a carboxylic acid group.

steps: Fizzing with carbonate shows a carboxylic acid, so it is ethanoic acid.
cards.why: Methyl methanoate is also C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>4</sub>O<sub>2</sub>, but an ester does not fizz with carbonates.

cards.q: Calculate the accurate relative molecular mass of ethanamide, \(\mathrm{C_{2}H_{5}NO}\), to four decimal places. (\(\mathrm{^{1}H}\) 1.0078, \(\mathrm{^{12}C}\) 12.0000, \(\mathrm{^{14}N}\) 14.0031, \(\mathrm{^{16}O}\) 15.9949)
cards.a: 59.0370
cards.why: Use the precise mass of the most common isotope of each element, not the relative atomic mass.

cards.q: What happens to a molecule when it absorbs infrared radiation?
cards.a: Its bonds vibrate more (stretch and bend). Each type of bond absorbs at characteristic wavenumbers.
cards.why: The wavenumber depends on the bond’s strength and the masses of the atoms it joins.

cards.q: In an infrared spectrum, what is plotted, and how does an absorption appear?
cards.a: Transmittance (%) against wavenumber (\(\text{cm}^{-1}\)). An absorption is a dip (trough) in transmittance.
cards.why: Wavenumber decreases from left to right on the x-axis, usually from 4000 to about 500 cm<sup>−1</sup>.

cards.q: What is the fingerprint region of an infrared spectrum, and how is it used?
cards.a: The region below about \(1500\ \text{cm}^{-1}\). Its complex pattern is unique to each compound, so comparing it with a database of known spectra identifies the molecule.
cards.why: Two compounds with the same functional groups still have different fingerprint regions.

cards.q: How do the IR spectra of an alcohol, an aldehyde and a carboxylic acid differ?
cards.a:
Alcohol: broad O–H absorption around \(3300\ \text{cm}^{-1}\), no C=O.
Aldehyde: strong C=O near \(1700\ \text{cm}^{-1}\), no O–H.
Carboxylic acid: very broad O–H from about 3300 to \(2500\ \text{cm}^{-1}\) and a C=O.
cards.why: The acid’s O–H is broadened by hydrogen bonding and overlaps the C–H absorptions.

cards.q: Propanal is made by oxidising propan-1-ol. How would an IR spectrum show whether the product still contains propan-1-ol?

figure.alt: Propan-1-ol is oxidised to propanal by acidified potassium dichromate, distilling off the aldehyde as it forms.

cards.a: Pure propanal has no O–H absorption. A broad O–H absorption around 3300 cm<sup>−1</sup> would show propan-1-ol is present as an impurity.
cards.why: IR can show that an impurity is present when it contains a bond the product does not.

cards.q: Propan-1-ol is heated under reflux with excess acidified potassium dichromate(VI). How does the IR spectrum change from starting material to product?

figure.alt: Propan-1-ol is oxidised to propanoic acid under reflux with acidified potassium dichromate.

cards.a: A C=O absorption appears near 1700 cm<sup>−1</sup>, and the O–H absorption becomes much broader, spreading to about 2500 cm<sup>−1</sup>.
cards.why: The product, propanoic acid, has both C=O and the very broad carboxylic acid O–H.

cards.q: Explain the link between the absorption of infrared radiation by \(\mathrm{CO_{2}}\), methane and water vapour and global warming.
cards.a: These gases absorb infrared radiation emitted by the Earth, trapping energy in the atmosphere.
marks: The Earth’s surface absorbs radiation from the Sun and re-emits it as infrared radiation.
Bonds in \(\mathrm{CO_{2}}\) (C=O), methane (C–H) and water (O–H) absorb this infrared radiation and vibrate.
The energy is re-emitted in all directions, some back towards the Earth, so less escapes to space.
Increasing concentrations of these gases trap more energy, causing global warming.

cards.q: Using the Edexcel Data Booklet, give the wavenumber ranges for O–H stretching in alcohols and in carboxylic acids.
cards.a: Alcohols: \(3750\text{–}3200\ \text{cm}^{-1}\). Carboxylic acids: \(3300\text{–}2500\ \text{cm}^{-1}\) (very broad).
cards.why: Strong hydrogen bonding between acid molecules makes their O–H absorption especially broad.

cards.q: Using the Edexcel Data Booklet, give the C=O stretching ranges for aldehydes, ketones and carboxylic acids (alkyl).
cards.a: Aldehydes (saturated alkyl) \(1740\text{–}1720\ \text{cm}^{-1}\); ketones (alkyl) \(1720\text{–}1700\ \text{cm}^{-1}\); carboxylic acids (alkyl) \(1725\text{–}1700\ \text{cm}^{-1}\).
cards.why: The ranges overlap, so a C=O absorption alone cannot tell these groups apart: look for O–H or the aldehyde C–H too.

cards.q: Using the Edexcel Data Booklet, which absorptions show an aldehyde rather than a ketone?
cards.a: The aldehyde C–H stretch: two absorptions at \(2900\text{–}2820\) and \(2775\text{–}2700\ \text{cm}^{-1}\).
cards.why: A ketone has no H on its carbonyl carbon, so it lacks these absorptions.

cards.q: Using the Edexcel Data Booklet, give the ranges for C=C stretching (isolated alkene), C–H stretching in alkenes and N–H stretching in amines.
cards.why: Alkane C–H is lower, \(2962\text{–}2853\ \text{cm}^{-1}\), so C–H just above \(3000\ \text{cm}^{-1}\) suggests an alkene.

cards.q: Predict the IR absorptions, with wavenumber ranges from the Edexcel Data Booklet, that would identify the functional groups in prop-2-en-1-ol.

figure.alt: Skeletal formula of prop-2-en-1-ol: a terminal C=C double bond, then a CH2 carrying an OH group.

cards.why: No absorption near 1700 cm<sup>−1</sup> is expected, because there is no C=O.

cards.q: True or false: an absorption near 1700 cm<sup>−1</sup> proves that a compound is a ketone.
cards.a: False. It shows a C=O bond, which is also in aldehydes, carboxylic acids, esters and amides.
cards.why: Use the other regions (O–H, aldehyde C–H) and other evidence to decide which carbonyl compound it is.

cards.q: True or false: a broad absorption around 3300 cm<sup>−1</sup> always means an alcohol is present.
cards.a: False. Carboxylic acids also have a broad O–H absorption, and N–H in amines absorbs in a similar region.
cards.why: Check for C=O (acid) and consider whether nitrogen is in the formula.

cards.q: Complete combustion of 0.600 g of compound Z (C, H and O only) gives 1.32 g of \(\mathrm{CO_{2}}\) and 0.720 g of \(\mathrm{H_{2}O}\). Find the empirical formula of Z. (\(M_{\text{r}}\): \(\mathrm{CO_{2}}\) 44.0, \(\mathrm{H_{2}O}\) 18.0; \(A_{\text{r}}\): C 12.0, H 1.0, O 16.0)
cards.a: \(\mathrm{C_{3}H_{8}O}\)
cards.why: All the carbon ends up in CO<sub>2</sub> and all the hydrogen in H<sub>2</sub>O; oxygen is found by difference.

cards.q: Z (\(\mathrm{C_{3}H_{8}O}\), molecular ion at \(m/z = 60\)) has a broad IR absorption at \(3350\ \text{cm}^{-1}\) and none near \(1700\ \text{cm}^{-1}\). Oxidising Z gives a product that forms a silver mirror with Tollens' reagent. Identify Z.
cards.a: Propan-1-ol

answerFigure.alt: Skeletal formula of propan-1-ol: a three-carbon chain with OH on the end carbon.

cards.why: M<sup>+</sup> 60 confirms the molecular formula; IR shows O–H and no C=O (an alcohol); oxidation to an aldehyde shows it is primary.

cards.q: A compound contains C 54.5%, H 9.1%, O 36.4% by mass. Its molecular ion is at \(m/z = 88\). Its IR spectrum shows a very broad absorption from 3300 to \(2500\ \text{cm}^{-1}\) and a strong one at \(1710\ \text{cm}^{-1}\). Suggest a structure. (\(A_{\text{r}}\): C 12.0, H 1.0, O 16.0)
cards.a: \(\mathrm{C_{4}H_{8}O_{2}}\), a carboxylic acid: butanoic acid (or 2-methylpropanoic acid).

answerFigure.alt: Skeletal formula of butanoic acid: a three-carbon chain joined to a carboxylic acid group.

steps: Very broad O–H plus C=O shows a carboxylic acid.
cards.why: More evidence, such as NMR, would be needed to decide between the two acid isomers.

cards.q: A compound \(\mathrm{C_{4}H_{8}O}\) has a strong IR absorption at \(1715\ \text{cm}^{-1}\), no broad O–H absorption, and gives no silver mirror with Tollens' reagent. Its mass spectrum has a large peak at \(m/z = 43\). Identify it.
cards.a: Butanone

answerFigure.alt: Skeletal formula of butanone: CH3 and CH2CH3 groups either side of a C=O.

cards.why: C=O but no O–H: an aldehyde or ketone. No silver mirror: a ketone. The only C4 ketone is butanone; 43 is CH<sub>3</sub>CO<sup>+</sup>.

cards.q: What does each technique mainly tell you when identifying an organic compound: test-tube reactions, mass spectrometry and infrared spectroscopy?
cards.a:
Test-tube reactions: which functional groups are present.
Mass spectrometry: the relative molecular mass (and, at high resolution, the molecular formula); fragments suggest parts of the structure.
IR: which bonds, and so which functional groups, are present.
cards.why: Each technique gives part of the answer; combining them identifies the compound.
